title: Blood Product Identification: Stop Before the Wrong Unit Starts
clientNeeds: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
bottomLine: Positive patient and blood-component identification is a critical transfusion safeguard. If identity, compatibility, order, product, or labeling does not align, do not start the transfusion.
recognize: Wrong-patient/wrong-unit errors can cause catastrophic hemolysis.
Electronic systems support safety but do not replace deliberate bedside verification.
priorities: Verify the patient, order, component, compatibility information, expiration, and required bedside checks exactly as policy requires.
assessMonitor: Confirm baseline symptoms and vital signs and that required access/equipment are ready.
interventions: Stop and resolve any mismatch before connecting the component.
medicationSafety: Blood-component administration authority varies by state/facility; PN/LVN participation must follow policy and competency.
teaching: Explain that repeated identity checks are intentional safety steps.
delegationScope: Bedside verification and transfusion initiation must follow licensed-role and institutional requirements.
examTrap: Starting because the unit number is close to the expected number.

title: Early Transfusion Monitoring: Stay Alert When Reactions Often Declare Themselves
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: The patient requires close observation after a blood component starts because acute reactions can develop rapidly. New fever, chills, pain, dyspnea, hypotension, or distress during transfusion is abnormal until evaluated.
recognize: Acute hemolysis, allergic reactions, TACO, TRALI, and bacterial contamination can present during or soon after transfusion.
priorities: Follow required bedside observation and vital-sign schedule and respond promptly to new symptoms.
assessMonitor: Trend temperature, BP, HR, respiratory status, oxygenation, pain, urine changes, and overall appearance.
interventions: Keep emergency supplies and escalation pathway accessible.
medicationSafety: Do not mask a developing reaction with routine symptom medication before evaluation unless specifically ordered for the situation.
teaching: Tell patients to report chills, itching, breathing difficulty, chest/back pain, nausea, or sudden anxiety immediately.
delegationScope: Monitoring frequency and transfusion staffing requirements follow policy; abnormal findings require licensed escalation.
examTrap: Leaving immediately after starting the component because baseline vitals were normal.
oneLinePearl: New symptoms during transfusion belong to the transfusion until proven otherwise.

title: Suspected Transfusion Reaction: Stop the Product and Escalate
clientNeeds: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
bottomLine: When a transfusion reaction is suspected, stop the blood component and activate the facility reaction protocol while supporting the patient. Do not restart the component until the reaction has been evaluated and policy explicitly permits it.
recognize: Fever, chills, flushing, urticaria, dyspnea, hypoxemia, chest/back pain, hypotension, nausea, dark urine, or acute distress can signal reaction.
priorities: Stop the transfusion, maintain patient safety/access per protocol, notify the required clinicians/blood bank, and recheck identity information.
assessMonitor: Trend ABCs, vital signs, oxygenation, urine output/color, rash, pain, and progression.
interventions: Follow specimen/component return and laboratory-workup instructions exactly.
medicationSafety: Reaction treatment is type-specific; do not assume an antihistamine is sufficient for respiratory failure, hemolysis, sepsis, or overload.
teaching: Explain that the transfusion is being stopped to evaluate a possible adverse reaction.
delegationScope: Reaction recognition and protocol activation require licensed nursing action; PN/LVN transfusion authority varies.
examTrap: Slowing the transfusion and waiting to see if symptoms resolve.
oneLinePearl: Suspected reaction: stop first, then sort out the type.

title: Acute Hemolytic Reaction: Think Identity Error and Hemolysis
bottomLine: Acute hemolytic transfusion reaction is a life-threatening emergency often associated with incompatibility. Fever/chills, back or flank pain, hypotension, chest discomfort, bleeding, or dark urine during transfusion require immediate reaction management.
recognize: Hemolysis may cause hemoglobinuria, renal injury, shock, or DIC.
priorities: Stop the component, support ABCs/circulation, and activate transfusion-reaction and blood-bank procedures.
assessMonitor: Trend hemodynamics, urine output/color, bleeding, temperature, pain, and ordered hemolysis/renal labs.
interventions: Preserve required blood/component and patient specimens for investigation.
medicationSafety: Do not restart the implicated unit.
teaching: Explain that incompatibility reactions are uncommon but require immediate investigation.
delegationScope: Emergency recognition/escalation are licensed responsibilities; treatment follows protocol/orders.
examTrap: Treating fever alone while continuing the component.
oneLinePearl: Hemolysis plus hypotension during transfusion is an emergency.
sourceBasis: CDC Hemovigilance acute hemolytic reaction framework

title: TACO: Transfusion Can Overload the Circulation
bottomLine: Transfusion-associated circulatory overload presents with respiratory distress and signs of volume overload temporally related to transfusion. Older adults and patients with cardiac or renal disease may be especially vulnerable.
recognize: Dyspnea, hypoxemia, hypertension, crackles, edema, JVD, or pulmonary edema during/after transfusion raise concern.
priorities: Stop or pause the component per reaction protocol, position/support breathing, and escalate promptly.
assessMonitor: Trend BP, oxygenation, lung findings, fluid balance, edema, and response to ordered treatment.
interventions: Follow transfusion-reaction protocol and ordered oxygen/diuretic/supportive care.
medicationSafety: Do not independently accelerate or modify future transfusion rates; prevention planning is provider/blood-bank/team based.
teaching: Patients with prior overload should ensure future teams know that history.
delegationScope: Volume-status interpretation and reaction escalation require licensed judgment.
examTrap: Assuming all transfusion-related dyspnea is allergic or TRALI.
oneLinePearl: TACO is too much circulatory volume, not simply 'a reaction rash.'

title: TRALI: Acute Lung Injury Without Simple Fluid Overload
bottomLine: TRALI is a serious transfusion-associated acute lung-injury syndrome. New hypoxemia and bilateral pulmonary findings around transfusion require immediate respiratory support and transfusion-reaction evaluation rather than reflexively assuming simple volume overload.
recognize: Acute dyspnea, hypoxemia, tachypnea, fever, and pulmonary infiltrates may occur.
priorities: Stop the transfusion, support oxygenation/ventilation, and activate reaction evaluation.
assessMonitor: Trend oxygenation, respiratory effort, hemodynamics, temperature, and imaging/labs as ordered.
interventions: Prepare for escalating respiratory support if deterioration continues.
medicationSafety: Diuretics are not automatically the answer to every transfusion-associated respiratory event; treatment depends on the diagnosis.
teaching: Explain that transfusion-related breathing problems require urgent evaluation even without rash.
delegationScope: Respiratory deterioration and transfusion-reaction escalation require licensed action.
examTrap: Giving a routine diuretic before differentiating TRALI from TACO and other causes.
oneLinePearl: TRALI is acute lung injury; TACO is circulatory overload.

title: Allergic Transfusion Reaction: Skin Findings Can Escalate to Airway Risk
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Itching or urticaria may be mild, but wheeze, angioedema, hypotension, or airway symptoms indicate severe allergic/anaphylactic reaction. Treat every new reaction according to transfusion protocol rather than guessing severity.
recognize: Hives, flushing, pruritus, wheeze, dyspnea, facial swelling, or hypotension can occur.
priorities: Stop the component and assess airway/breathing/circulation before medication treatment.
assessMonitor: Monitor rash progression, airway, BP, oxygenation, and response to ordered therapy.
interventions: Follow reaction protocol and prepare emergency treatment for anaphylaxis when indicated.
medicationSafety: Do not restart a component after a suspected reaction unless the required evaluation is complete and policy/order permits.
teaching: Report even mild itching promptly because severity can progress.
delegationScope: Reaction assessment/escalation requires licensed nursing action.
examTrap: Giving diphenhydramine while the transfusion continues.
oneLinePearl: Skin symptoms are not harmless if the airway or blood pressure is changing.

title: Septic Transfusion Reaction: Fever and Rigors Can Mean Contamination
clientNeeds: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
bottomLine: High fever, rigors, hypotension, nausea/vomiting, or shock during transfusion can represent bacterial contamination and sepsis. Stop the component and activate the transfusion-reaction/sepsis pathway immediately.
recognize: Rapid systemic toxicity during transfusion is not a routine febrile response.
priorities: Stop the transfusion, support ABCs/circulation, notify required teams, and follow culture/component investigation procedures.
assessMonitor: Trend temperature, hemodynamics, mental status, oxygenation, urine output, lactate/labs as ordered.
interventions: Prepare for cultures, antibiotics, fluids, and higher-level care per sepsis orders/protocol.
medicationSafety: Do not suppress fever and continue the component while awaiting reassessment.
teaching: Explain that contaminated-product reactions are rare but time-sensitive.
delegationScope: Recognition and immediate escalation require licensed nursing action.
examTrap: Calling rigors 'expected chills' and continuing transfusion.
oneLinePearl: Fever plus shock during transfusion is sepsis until proven otherwise.

title: Febrile Nonhemolytic Reaction: Fever Still Requires Evaluation
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Fever/chills during transfusion may ultimately be a febrile nonhemolytic reaction, but hemolysis and bacterial contamination must be considered first. Follow the reaction protocol rather than self-classifying it as benign.
recognize: Temperature rise and chills may occur without hemolysis, but early presentations overlap with more dangerous reactions.
priorities: Stop/hold the component per policy and perform the required reaction assessment/workup.
assessMonitor: Trend temperature, BP, pain, urine changes, rigors, and systemic toxicity.
interventions: Use ordered antipyretic treatment only after appropriate evaluation.
medicationSafety: Premedication practices are order/policy specific and do not eliminate the need to assess new fever.
teaching: Report fever/chills immediately even if a prior transfusion caused similar symptoms.
examTrap: Assuming previous mild fever means this episode is also benign.
oneLinePearl: A transfusion fever earns evaluation before reassurance.

title: Transfusion History Handoff: Prior Reactions Must Follow the Patient
clientNeeds: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Coordinated Care
bottomLine: Prior transfusion reactions, antibodies, special blood requirements, and transfusion-related overload history are critical handoff information. Missing this history can increase future risk.
recognize: Patients may remember 'a bad reaction' without knowing the type; records/blood-bank history may provide essential detail.
priorities: Reconcile previous reactions and special component requirements before future transfusion.
assessMonitor: Confirm documented reaction type, date, component, treatment, and future precautions when available.
interventions: Communicate relevant history during transfers and discharge follow-up.
medicationSafety: Do not assume routine premedication prevents serious reactions or substitutes for special-component requirements.
teaching: Encourage patients to tell every care team about prior transfusion problems.
delegationScope: History collection can be shared, but interpretation and transfusion planning require licensed/blood-bank collaboration.
examTrap: Documenting 'allergy to blood' without clarifying the prior event.
oneLinePearl: A transfusion history is medication history-level safety information.
